analysis.one_liner: Exempts shipping to Hawaii, Alaska, and Puerto Rico from Jones Act rules when competition is thin.
analysis.headline: The bill received no cosponsors, never left the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee, and died when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021 without any vote.
analysis.plain_summary: A federal law known as the Jones Act requires that ships carrying goods between U.S. ports be built in America, mostly U.S.-owned, and largely crewed by U.S. citizens. Because only a few shipping lines operate those routes, shipping to places like Hawaii, Alaska, and Puerto Rico costs more than shipping to foreign ports. This bill would lift those requirements on a route unless at least three independent companies each carry at least a fifth of the goods on that route. No committee ever took it up, and it expired when the two-year Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers, businesses, and governments in Puerto Rico, Hawaii, and Alaska, who pay some of the highest shipping rates in the world under the Jones Act and would likely see lower rates if more carriers could enter their routes. Retailers importing food, fuel, and goods to those areas would also pay less.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Residents of Puerto Rico, Hawaii, and Alaska

how_it_helps.text: The bill removes the Jones Act's U.S.-build, U.S.-ownership, and U.S.-crew requirements on a noncontiguous route unless three independent operators each carry at least 20 percent of that route's volume, a threshold intended to allow foreign competition only where the market is dominated by fewer players [S2] [S3].

The Jones Act is widely cited as raising shipping costs to Puerto Rico, Hawaii, and Alaska relative to ports served by foreign carriers; exempting thin routes would expose the incumbent lines to price competition [S2].

analysis.who_pays: U.S.-flagged shipping companies serving noncontiguous routes, the U.S. shipyards that build their vessels, and American merchant mariners whose jobs depend on the crewing mandate. Proponents of the Jones Act also argue the law supports national security by keeping a U.S. shipbuilding base and trained seafaring workforce available in emergencies.
analysis.who_pays_short: Jones Act shipping lines and U.S. shipyards

drawbacks.text: Ending Jones Act requirements on these routes would reduce demand for U.S.-built, U.S.-crewed vessels, threatening shipyard jobs and the pool of American merchant mariners that national-security planning relies on [S2].
The bill sets a competition test — three independent operators each carrying 20 percent of a route — that could be difficult to meet or game, leaving the actual effect on rates uncertain [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Lower shipping costs for island and Alaska households and businesses would be a real, measurable gain, since transport costs feed directly into food and consumer prices. The cost is real too: fewer U.S.-built ships and less work for American crews, with national-security implications that defenders of the Jones Act take seriously. The bill is a targeted exemption rather than a full repeal, which limits both the savings and the damage.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and then its maritime subcommittee, never received a single cosponsor, and expired when the 116th Congress ended without a hearing, markup, or floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Ed Case (D-HI) introduced the bill on December 19, 2019, and it was referred to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee that same day [S1] [S5].
The next day it was referred to the Subcommittee on Coast Guard and Maritime Transportation, which was the last action the bill ever received [S5].
No member cosponsored the bill [S4], and no vote was ever held before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The outcome preserves the status quo: U.S.-flagged carriers and shipyards keep their Jones Act protection and the higher rates it sustains, while consumers in Puerto Rico, Hawaii, and Alaska continue paying the same shipping costs. With no cosponsors and no committee action, the bill's failure says as much about the political difficulty of touching the Jones Act as about anything else.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Jones Act carriers, shipyards, and merchant mariners

for.name: Rep. Ed Case
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and gave introductory remarks, targeting shipping costs to his home state of Hawaii.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and no member from either party cosponsored the bill, so no partisan pattern exists in the record.

industries.note: These carriers hold a legal monopoly-like position on noncontiguous routes and charge rates well above foreign-ship benchmarks. The bill would strip that protection wherever fewer than three independent carriers operate.
The Jones Act requires U.S.-built vessels for domestic routes, guaranteeing shipyards a captive domestic market. Exempting routes would shrink that guaranteed demand.

industries.industry: American merchant mariners and maritime unions
industries.note: Crewing mandates protect mariner jobs and wages, which national-security shipactivations depend on; exempting routes would reduce that workforce, though consumers elsewhere gain from lower rates.
